P01.passage: From 1951 to 1966 a chemist at a small university laboratory worked with a single technician, a young woman hired straight out of high school. For her first year she only washed glassware. The chemist then had her run each step of his syntheses while he corrected her hands, and repeat them until she could work without him; when he retired, she took over the laboratory and went on using his methods. One biographer has described the technician as, more than anything, the chemist's ______.
P01.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P02.passage: From 1884 to 1910 a mining valley's only newspaper was a four-page weekly sold at the pithead for a penny. For most miners it was the only news they saw, and each issue printed reports of distant strikes, tariffs, and elections, each followed by a column explaining what it would mean for men working underground. Diaries and union minutes from the valley in those years discuss faraway events almost always in that column's own terms and examples. Writing a century later, one historian called the weekly the miners' ______.
P02.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P03.passage: From 1820 to 1860 a mountain village was governed by a council of four elected members, who appointed a secretary to keep the minutes of their meetings. The secretary sat beside the chairman at every meeting, drafted the chairman's letters, and kept the chairman's seal. When the chairman fell ill in 1838 and again in 1845, the secretary ran the council's meetings for months at a time. When the chairman died in 1851, the members made the secretary chairman without a contest. In the village's records, one historian has argued, the secretary appears above all as the council's ______.
P03.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P04.passage: In 1712 a market town ordered every household to send one adult each spring to spend two days clearing the town's drainage ditches, or else to pay a fine of one shilling. In the 1850s the council laid covered brick drains beneath the streets, and the old ditches were filled in and built over. The rule was never repealed and still stands in the town's printed code, though the clerk last called the spring muster in 1858. By 1900, one historian observes, the ditch rule had become ______.
P04.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P05.passage: In 2015 a city passed an ordinance limiting where street vendors could park their carts. Under the earlier rules, an inspector who found a cart in the wrong place had simply asked its owner to move along. The ordinance let inspectors choose among a warning, a fine, and towing, and in the first year they towed in nine of every ten cases, holding each cart for thirty days; by year's end about a third of the city's licensed vendors had left the trade. Asked about its first year, most of the vendors interviewed for one study described the city's enforcement of the ordinance as ______.
P05.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P06.passage: In 1560 an empire seized a small island port at the mouth of a strait, a place with thin soil and almost no trade of its own. The empire's fleets on the long ocean crossing could carry only a few weeks of water and grain. In the calm months merchants shipped grain, salted meat, and spare timber to the island, where they were stacked in warehouses built along the harbor. In the storm months, when no merchant ship could reach the island, the fleets put in there and loaded what had been gathered. For the next century, one historian has argued, the empire valued the island chiefly as its ______.
P06.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P07.passage: A small town lies forty miles north of a large port city, on a railway line opened in 1890. In the 1910s the railway added an early train south to the city and an evening train back, and cut the fare for monthly ticket holders. The town's own mills and shops closed one by one as new houses spread over its old fields, and by the late 1920s most of its adults boarded the 6:40 train every weekday morning and were not seen on its streets again until evening. By 1930, one regional planner observed, the town had in effect become the city's ______.
P07.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P08.passage: For most of the eighteenth century, two towns on opposite banks of a salmon river tore down each other's fish weirs whenever the run was good. In 1790 the two councils signed a truce at a feast on the bridge, and they renewed it with the same toasts every spring until 1815. The magistrates' books for those years record cut weirs on both banks at about the rate of the decades before. Neither council fined a single man for crossing to the far bank, and the feast grew larger every year. Writing a century later, one historian called the truce between the towns from 1790 to 1815 ______.
P08.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P09.passage: From 1878 to 1901 a single inspector examined the cargo landed at a small river port for the customs service. Merchants' letters complain that the gifts of wine and banknotes that eased crates through other ports on the river came back to them from his, and he sent each such offer, with the giver's name, to his superiors. Several captains who had made offers were prosecuted on his reports. Reading his reports a century later, one historian described the inspector as ______.
P09.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P10.passage: In 1928 a record company made the first recording of an old ballad from the hill counties, about a ferryman drowned in a flood. No collector in the hill counties had found it before 1928. The singer on the record had learned it as a child from an aunt, the last person in her valley who knew it, and sang every verse to the aunt's tune in the aunt's hard, plain style. Within two years singers at fairs and churches across the state had taken it up. One folklorist has argued that the 1928 recording had ______ the ballad.
P10.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P11.passage: For centuries the villages of one mountain valley marked the end of the olive harvest with a night procession, led by singers, from the church to the presses. In 1951 a national law listed the procession among forty "living monuments" of the country. The law closed the route to traffic on each harvest night, paid the villages to repair the presses and lanterns, and forbade any authority to alter or ban the event, so the procession went on as it always had while similar customs in neighboring valleys lapsed. Writing in 1990, one folklorist concluded that the changes of the previous fifty years had ______ the custom.
P11.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P12.passage: In 1922 two neighboring states signed a treaty dividing the water of a river that crossed both, and much of its later history turned on its seventh clause. That clause let the downstream state stop its yearly payment toward the upstream state's dam in any year the river ran short. The river seldom ran short. In forty years the downstream state never stopped a payment, and its officials raised the clause whenever they wanted a highway link, a share of a power plant, or fishing rights, and the upstream state gave way each time. Writing in 1980, one legal historian called the seventh clause the treaty's ______.
P12.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P13.passage: In 1952 a state marketing board began buying the reed baskets that households on a small fishing island had woven for generations. Until then nearly every household had woven its own baskets on winter evenings for its own boats. The board bought only from weavers who held its certificate, which took two years of full-time training at its workshop, and it paid them a monthly wage. By 1975 the island's baskets came from about thirty weavers, and the crews bought theirs at the board's depot. Visiting the island in 1975, one folklorist concluded that the board's purchases had ______ the craft.
P13.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P14.passage: A weavers' guild built a stone hall beside the market square of a river town in 1580, and the guild was dissolved in 1760. No buyer could be found for the building, and within forty years it had lost its roof and most of its upper walls. A survey of the town in 1860 found stones bearing the guild's carved emblem in the foundations of more than sixty houses and in the bridge over the millrace. In the century after 1760, one historian writes, the hall served chiefly as the town's ______.
P14.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P15.passage: In the spring of 1974 a river broke through its levees and flooded some four hundred homes in a farming district. The ministry acted within a day, sending trucks of sandbags and a check for one fixed sum to every household. A family whose cellar had taken a foot of water received what a family whose house had washed away received, and the sandbags were tipped out at the roadside, unfilled and unstacked, for each household to place itself. In a later account, one reporter described the national ministry's response to the flood as ______.
P15.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P16.passage: From 1880 to 1930 the weekly paper of a small river city carried an unsigned column on its front page. The city had no railway until 1928, and the column's author read the foreign newspapers that reached the river port by steamer, weeks late. Each week he summarized wars, elections and inventions abroad, and diaries from the period show families learning of the telephone, the deaths of distant kings and the outbreak of war in Europe from his column before any other source. One historian of the city calls the column, over the fifty years it ran, the city's ______.
P16.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P17.passage: In 1871 the hand-loom weavers of a hill district pooled their dues to buy a stone hall in the market town. Its upper room held evening classes in bookkeeping, drafting, and shorthand, taught by members' children who worked in the city. The classes were always full, and the weavers' records show most who finished them leaving the looms within a few years for city offices. Membership fell every decade, and the dues of those who remained went largely to paying the teachers. For the next half century, one historian has argued, the hall served the district's weavers chiefly as their ______.
P17.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P18.passage: In 1907 a composer built one movement of his first symphony on a folk tune he had heard in a fishing village. In the village a single fiddler played it, with nothing beneath it. In the symphony the violins carry it note for note from start to finish while the cellos play a second village tune below, and the two lines cross and recross so that each is heard more clearly against the other. Comparing the symphony with the village version, one critic observed that the composer had ______ the tune.
P18.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P19.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the storm still rises and the sailor is washed ashore alive, walking home to his mother's door. The verse in which his body is found appears in none of them, and the closing verse, once a curse on the sea, now thanks it for sparing him. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
P19.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P20.passage: In 1958 a retired wheat farmer published a memoir of his forty years on the plains, with a chapter for each season of the farm year. In his pages a summer sunrise over the stubble is "a blaze of molten brass poured upon a tapestry of gold," and milking a cow becomes "the patient summoning of a pale and foaming fountain." Every other chore of the farm year, from mending fences to hauling grain to market, is dressed in the same heaped adjectives and metaphors. Critics who reviewed the book found its prose ______ from first chapter to last.
P20.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P21.passage: In 1948 a new regional health board took charge of every hospital in a rural county, among them the old stone county hospital. The board needed land beside its new city hospital, and the state university, which owned the plot there, had a medical school that wanted a teaching building in the county. In 1952 the board signed the county hospital over to the medical school, and its accounts for that year record no payment received. That same month the university's plot passed to the board. Writing about the board's first decade, one historian of medicine concluded that the board had ______ the county hospital.
P21.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P22.passage: In the spring of 1936 a flood swept the length of a narrow farming valley, where a river had run for centuries between orchards and cornfields to a rocky gorge at the valley's lower end. The water rose slowly, leaving nearly every barn and house standing, and it lay on the fields for six weeks, leaving behind a crust of salt carried up from the coastal marshes. Nothing planted in the next three springs would grow, and by 1946 the census counted twelve families in the valley where there had been ninety. Revisiting the valley a decade later, one geographer wrote that the flood had ______ it.
P22.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P23.passage: For thirty-one years a single critic wrote the weekly theater column of a city newspaper. Starting in 1920, her reviews of comedies, tragedies, and musicals alike ended with a sentence about what standing room cost the city's clerks and shopgirls. A later index of her columns finds that sentence in all but a handful of the reviews she wrote over the next eleven years. Theater managers' letters from 1931 name her column when the three largest theaters halved standing-room prices, and the closing sentences stopped the following week. Having read the full run of her reviews, one theater historian described the critic as ______.
P23.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P24.passage: A state forestry service founded in 1911 managed the timber of a mountainous province, and one of its fourteen districts was a narrow valley in the eastern hills. Every other district lay west of a river that had no bridge until 1940, and the valley was the only one beyond it. The service kept a small station there, staffed by foresters sent from the capital for two years at a time, who issued cutting permits for the whole eastern hills and sent their reports back by courier. One historian argues that, from 1911 to 1940, the valley was above all the service's ______.
P24.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P25.passage: In 1871 the fishermen of a small harbor village on a rocky coast pooled their savings to open a boatyard. Few fishermen there had cash, and the nearest bank lay two days inland. A buyer could launch his boat at once and hand the yard a fifth of every season's catch. The yard's accounts show those shares stopping in the season the hull's price had been reached, often eight or ten years after its launch, and by 1921 most boats on that coast had been launched this way. Looking back on its first fifty years, one historian argued that the yard had served the coast above all as its ______.
P25.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P26.passage: In 1782 a trading house from the coast opened an office in a river town where farmers from the surrounding district had long sold their grain. The house never bought or sold a sack of grain itself. Each spring the forty small dealers who bought from the farmers borrowed from it, and they repaid it with interest after the millers downriver had paid them. In 1794, when the house shut its office for one season, half of the dealers could not buy a harvest at all. One economic historian has argued that by 1800 the house had ______ the town's grain trade.
P26.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P27.passage: Above a harbor town, a river crosses six miles of reedy marsh, and below the marsh the lower river runs past the town's quays to the bay. In wet springs the river soaks into the marsh's deep peat, and gauges below the marsh rise only half as far as gauges above it. Through the dry summer the peat lets the water out again a little at a time. The lower river keeps flowing past the quays in months when the river above the marsh shrinks to a chain of pools. One hydrologist has concluded that the marsh serves the lower river as a kind of ______.
P27.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P28.passage: In 1868 the twenty-four football clubs of a northern county's league, from its towns and villages alike, adopted a new rule for their matches. It let a side that caught the ball keep it for as long as its forwards could hold off a tackle. Clubs from the colliery villages, whose forwards were the heaviest men in the county, won fifty-one of their next sixty matches. A title that had changed hands nearly every year went to one of three colliery clubs in each of the next twelve seasons. Looking back, one sports historian argued that the rule of 1868 had ______ the game.
P28.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P29.passage: In 1880 a geologist proposed that the hot springs of a mountain basin were fed by rain falling on a ridge to the north. The 1931 survey set out to test the idea, and its first borehole struck a body of molten rock less than two miles down, far shallower than anyone had thought possible. The papers that followed over the next decade concerned the molten rock, and the dye tests planned for the ridge were never carried out. One historian of geology writes that the 1931 survey ______ the ridge hypothesis.
P29.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P30.passage: In 1968 a city opened a new central library, designed by a young architect, on the site of an old train station. The architect had given its reading rooms no fixed walls in the plans: the shelves ran on floor tracks, and the partitions hung from ceiling rails. Before the year was out, the staff had turned the music room into a children's library and then into an exhibition hall, each time over a single weekend and without calling in builders. Reviewing it that year, one critic called the building, above all, ______.
P30.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P31.passage: For six centuries a small monastery stood at the top of the only pass between two mountain valleys, each ruled by its own lord. The lords spoke different languages and, after a long war, would let none of each other's envoys into their valleys. Monks who knew both tongues carried each lord's offers over the pass and back, proposed terms on grazing rights and on marriages between the two houses, and saw the treaties that kept the peace for two centuries drafted in the monastery's hall. In a history of the pass, one scholar described the monastery as, above all, the region's ______.
P31.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P32.passage: Since 1985 foresters have surveyed a stand of oaks on a dry ridge every summer, and in the early 1990s an outbreak struck it. The outbreak was a root fungus, which rots the thick roots that anchor an oak while its trunk stays sound and its crown stays in full leaf. As the rot spread, the surveys measured the oaks leaning a little further each year. By 2005 they recorded open ground where the stand had been, with the trunks lying across it, each still attached to a rotted mass of roots. Summing up three decades of surveys, one forester wrote that the outbreak had ______ the oaks.
P32.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P33.passage: In 1790 a country surveyor published a map of the kingdom that went through eleven printings in twenty years. Rival maps copied their coastlines and roads from older charts, errors and all. The surveyor walked every main road with a measuring chain and fixed each town by sightings of the stars, and when the government's survey checked his sheets with better instruments sixty years later, few of his distances were off by more than a mile. Comparing it with other maps of its day, one historian describes the surveyor's map as, above all, ______.
P33.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P34.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. He edited a literary weekly there and reviewed each of her books in it when it appeared, naming the weak lines and the forced rhymes. Her later notebooks show her reworking exactly the poems he had faulted, and the second editions differ from the first at the lines his reviews had quoted. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
P34.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P35.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. He appears in only one chapter, the eleventh of twenty-two, when he tells the magistrate that the old master signed a later will. In the ten chapters before it, the sisters' fortunes rise as their claim to the estate gains support; in the eleven after it, a cousin's lawsuit built on that later will strips them of nearly everything. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
P35.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P36.passage: In 1974 a state commission published a report on the last dam on the river, which had stood for sixty years. Removal had been argued for a decade, with both sides citing a single engineering estimate of its cost. The commission offered three new estimates that differed tenfold and two incompatible counts of the salmon the river could support. Afterward each side quoted in the state's papers whichever figure suited it, and legislators, saying they could no longer tell what removal would cost, put off the vote they had scheduled. In her history of the river, one journalist wrote that the report had ______ the debate over the dam.
P36.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P37.passage: In the 1920s an amateur naturalist began studying the bluebirds that nested in forty wooden boxes along the fences of her family's farm. The boxes were too dark to see into without lifting the lid, which sent the parents flying. She fixed a dentist's mirror to a knitting needle and, holding a flashlight beside the entrance hole, slid the mirror inside and counted the eggs in its reflection without touching the box. Biologists decades later adopted the same trick for nest boxes of every size. In a review of early bird studies, one biologist called the naturalist's approach ______.
P37.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P38.passage: For most of the 1960s a retired surgeon sat on the nine-member board of trustees of a county hospital. She was the board's chair for the whole decade, and her name headed its letterhead. The bylaws gave the chair no vote except to break a tie, and the agenda and the budget were drawn up each year by the hospital's administrator, whose recommendations the other eight trustees adopted at nearly every meeting; in ten years no vote ever ended in a tie. In an oral history recorded decades later, one fellow trustee called her the board's ______ during those years.
P38.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P39.passage: When a novelist died in 1931, she left the manuscript of her last novel, a story of dockworkers' families set in the 1880s, to her longtime editor. The editor printed it in 1932. In that edition horse carts have become trucks, the dockers earn the wages of 1932, and the closing strike follows the course of the great strike that readers still remembered. Every chapter of the manuscript is present in the printed book, which reviewers praised as a portrait of the present-day waterfront. In a study published decades later, one scholar argued that this editor had ______ the book.
P39.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

P40.passage: In 1882 a forty-page pamphlet on the rights of tenant farmers appeared in one rural province, the same year a tenants' movement formed there. Its author, a village schoolteacher, argued that land belongs by right to those who work it, and the movement's speakers quoted its chapters to settle every dispute over aims. When a branch secretary published an essay in 1887 questioning one chapter, his branch expelled him within the month, and no member criticized the pamphlet in print again before 1892. Looking back, one historian called the pamphlet the movement's ______ in its first decade.
P40.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
